slides.notes:
So in today’s session, let’s start with the Agenda.we’ll understand Interfaces – GUI vs CLI – and see why CLI is important.After that, we’ll check what a Shell is, and explore the Types of Shells.Next, we will see some key Commands, Bash  to tie everything together.
 Finally, we’ll end with basic commands like ls, history, and whoami etc. to get comfortable.

slides.title: User Interface
slides.body:
Graphical User Interface
Graphical User Interface (GUI) commonly referred as the User Interface (UI)
slides.notes:
Now, let’s move ahead and talk about User Interfaces. A common type is the Graphical User Interface, or GUI, which many people simply call the User Interface (UI). It’s the point where users interact with the system visually.
Can you think of some everyday examples of GUI that you use?icons, menus, buttons, windows, and scrollbars used in systems like computers, mobiles, and apps.

slides.title: User Interface
slides.body:
Command User Interface
Command Line Interface (CLI) facilitates the users to perform powerful operations on a computer with simple commands
Command is a text instruction to a computer program to perform a specific task
slides.notes:
Next, let’s understand the Command Line Interface (CLI).
Unlike GUI, the CLI allows users to perform powerful operations using simple text commands.
A command is nothing but a text instruction that tells the computer to perform a specific task.

slides.title: Command Line Interface
slides.body:
What is Shell?
ib-developer@cloud:~$
Bash
Shell is the software that interprets and executes the various commands that we provide
Terminal is a text input/output environment
slides.notes: Alright, moving ahead from the Command Line Interface, let’s talk about the Shell. The Shell is the software that interprets and executes the commands we type. It usually runs inside a Terminal, which is the text input/output environment where we interact.

slides.title: Shell
slides.body:
Different Shells
Bourne Shell (sh)
Bourne-Again Shell (bash)
C Shell (csh)
Korn Shell (ksh)
Z Shell (zsh)
slides.notes: Now that we know what a Shell is, let’s look at the different types of shells available. Some common ones are the Bourne Shell (sh), the Bourne-Again Shell (bash), the C Shell (csh), the Korn Shell (ksh), and the Z Shell (zsh).

slides.title: Command Line Interface
slides.body:
Opening Terminal
Open the Dash (Super Key) or Applications and type terminal
Shortcut:  Ctrl + Alt + T
Bash is one of the most commonly used shell in Linux distributions
slides.notes:
Now, Moving on, with how to actually open the Terminal.
We know that Bash is one of the most commonly used shells in Linux distributions.
To open the terminal, you can go to the Dash or Applications menu and type “terminal”.
An easier way is the shortcut Ctrl + Alt + T.

slides.title: Command Line Interface
slides.body:
Opening Terminal
Open Launchpad and search for terminal.
Press command(⌘) + space, type "terminal"
slides.notes: Alright, stepping ahead with how to open the Terminal on macOS. You can simply open Launchpad and search for “terminal”. Or, a quicker way is pressing Command (⌘) + Space, typing “terminal”, and hitting enter.

slides.title: Shell
slides.body:
Alternatively you can use Google Cloud Shell
https://shell.cloud.google.com/ 
Using Cloud
Alternatively you can use Google Cloud Shell
https://shell.cloud.google.com/
slides.notes: Now,going forward, there’s also an alternative to installing anything locally. You can use the Google Cloud Shell, available at shell.cloud.google.com. It gives you a ready-to-use shell environment directly in the browser.

slides.title: Terminal
slides.body:
Bash
ib-developer@cloud:~$
Cursor/shell is ready to take the commands
username
Bash
slides.notes: Alright,next, let’s take a closer look at the Bash terminal. Here, you can see the username displayed, followed by the prompt — for example, ib-developer@cloud:~$. This indicates that the shell is ready to take commands. So, whenever you see this prompt and the blinking cursor, it means the system is waiting for your input.

slides.title: Commands
slides.notes: let’s move ahead and talk about Commands.

slides.title: Commands
slides.body:
Listing Files & Directories
 ls  is used to list files and directories
ib-developer@cloud:~$ ls
apj_codes             'matrix rotation'
code                   Music
Bash
slides.notes: Now, the ls command in Linux lists all files and directories in your current working directory.For example, here typing ls may show items like apj_codes, matrix rotation, code, and Music.It’s useful to confirm whether a file exists or to quickly see what’s inside a folder.Think of it as the command-line version of opening a folder in File Explorer or Finder.

slides.title: Commands
slides.body:
Get Options for Commands
 help  displays a list of options that you can use with the command
ib-developer@cloud:~$ ls --help
-a, --all                  do not ignore entries starting with .
-A, --almost-all           do not list implied . and ..
    --author               with -l, print the author of each file
...
Bash
slides.notes:
Stepping ahead, let’s learn how to get options for commands. Every command has extra options or flags, and we can see them by adding --help.
For example, typing ls --help shows a list of options like -a to display hidden files or -A to list almost all files etc…. This is a quick way to explore what more a command can do.

slides.title: Commands
slides.body:
Get Current User
 whoami  displays the current logged in user
ib-developer@cloud:~$ whoami  
ib-developer
Bash
slides.notes:
Alright, moving ahead, let’s look at the whoami command. This command is used to display the current logged-in user.
For example, when we type whoami, the output here is ib-developer, which means that’s the username currently active in the system.
It’s a simple but very useful command when working on shared systems or remote servers.

slides.title: Commands
slides.body:
Previous Commands
Shell keeps track of the commands you have typed in. Use up (   ) and down (   ) arrows to access the commands
slides.notes:
Now, let’s see how the shell helps us with previous commands. The shell automatically keeps track of everything we type. Instead of retyping, we can use the up and down arrow keys to scroll through our command history and reuse them.
This saves time, especially when running long or repeated commands.
Have you tried using the arrow keys in your terminal before?

slides.title: Commands
slides.body:
History
ib-developer@cloud:~$ history
1 ls
2 ls --help 
3 whoami
…
Bash
 history  display the history of the commands you have typed in so far.  By default, It shows the last 500 recent commands
slides.notes:
Alright, moving ahead, let’s talk about the history command. This command shows a list of all the commands you have typed in so far. By default, it usually displays the last 500 commands.
For example, in the output shown, you can see commands like ls, ls --help, and whoami with their line numbers. This is very useful when you want to repeat or review what you’ve done earlier without typing everything again.

slides.title: Commands
slides.body:
Clear
 clear  command clears the terminal
ib-developer@cloud:~$
Shortcut: Ctrl+L
ib-developer@cloud:~$ history
1 ls
2 ls --help
3 whoami
ib-developer@cloud:~$ clear
slides.notes: The clear command erases everything on the terminal, giving you a clean workspace. For example, after viewing past commands with history, typing clear refreshes the screen, leaving only the prompt. You can also use the shortcut Ctrl + L for the same result.

slides.title: Commands
slides.body:
alias
alias defines a shortcut for a longer command
ib-developer@cloud:~$ alias cls='clear'
slides.notes:
Alright, let’s look at something really handy — aliases.An alias is like creating a shortcut for a longer command. For example, typing clear again and again might feel repetitive. So, instead, we can set up an alias: alias cls='clear' .
Now, every time we type cls, it works just like clear.
Quick check for you: what other commands do you think you might want to create shortcuts for in your daily work?"

slides.title: Commands
slides.body:
unalias
unalias clear custom aliases defined with the alias command
ib-developer@cloud:~$ unalias cls
slides.notes:
Now let’s look at the unalias command. We use unalias when we want to remove or clear a custom alias that we previously defined.
For example, earlier we created an alias cls for clear. If we don’t need it anymore, running unalias cls will delete that shortcut. After this, typing cls will no longer work.

slides.title: Commands
slides.body:
Exit
ib-developer@cloud:~$ exit
Bash
 exit  to close/end a shell session
slides.notes:
Now, we wrap up the section on commands, let’s learn how to end a shell session. The command for this is simply exit.
When you type exit in the terminal, it immediately closes the shell session and takes you back to the normal system interface.
So remember — just type exit to close the terminal session.

slides.title: Commands
slides.body: Summary
slides.notes:
Alright, let’s quickly recap the commands we learned:
ls to list files and directories
--help to check options for commands
whoami to display the current user
history to view the last 500 commands
tables: Displays list of options for a given command
It will show you the last five hundred commands you have entered.

slides.title: Commands
slides.body: Summary
slides.notes:
Then we also have 
clear to clean the terminal screen
Alias to define a shortcut for a longer command
Unalias to clear custom aliases defined with the alias command
exit to close the shell session
These simple commands are the building blocks of working with the command line.
